question_text:
Lichenometry is a dating method in which the diameter of the largest lichen on a rock surface is used to estimate how long ago the surface was exposed. Geomorphologist Ingrid Salvesen measured the largest lichen on each of ten boulders deposited at the edge of a retreating glacier, whose exposure ages were known from survey records. The graph shows each boulder's lichen diameter (in millimeters) plotted against its exposure age (in years), along with a fitted line. Salvesen concluded that the fitted line is a less dependable guide to lichen diameter for the older boulders than for the younger ones.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Salvesen's conclusion?
answer_a: Lichen diameters are generally larger on older boulders than on younger ones, and the points for the oldest boulders and the youngest boulders alike fall close to the fitted line.
answer_b: The points for boulders younger than 50 years fall both above and below the fitted line by wide margins, whereas the points for boulders 50 years and older fall close to it.
answer_c: The points for boulders older than 50 years fall both above and below the fitted line by wide margins, whereas the points for boulders 50 years and younger fall close to it.
answer_d: The points for boulders older than 30 years fall both above and below the fitted line by wide margins, whereas the points for the three youngest boulders fall close to it.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it accurately describes how the points sit relative to the fitted line for the older and younger boulders. Salvesen concluded that the line is a less dependable guide for the older boulders, which means the older points should lie farther from the line. In the graph, the five boulders older than 50 years (60, 70, 80, 90, and 100 years) are scattered on both sides of the line by large margins, some well above it and some well below it, while the five boulders that are 50 years old or younger lie almost exactly on it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. Its first clause is accurate for the sample overall, since the fitted line rises, but its second clause is not: the points for the oldest boulders lie far from the line, so this choice describes a trend across the whole set and does not support the conclusion that the line is less dependable for older boulders.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it reverses the two groups. The points for boulders younger than 50 years lie very close to the fitted line, and it is the points for the older boulders that lie far from it.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it draws the dividing line at the wrong age. The points for the 40-year-old and 50-year-old boulders lie almost exactly on the fitted line, so the wide scatter above and below the line begins only with the boulders older than 50 years, not those older than 30 years.

question_text:
An adult-education coordinator evaluated a twelve-week oral reading fluency program offered at five community centers. At each center, participants' average oral reading speed, in words per minute, was measured at enrollment and again at the end of the program. Reviewing the results, the coordinator concluded that the program's effect was proportionally largest at the center whose participants began with the lowest average reading speed.

Which choice best describes data from the table that support the coordinator's conclusion?
answer_a: Elm Street had the highest reading speed after the program, and its participants gained more words per minute than Alder Park's participants did.
answer_b: Cedar Hill's participants gained more words per minute than any other center's participants, and they began with a lower average speed than the participants at Dunmore Road and Elm Street.
answer_c: Relative to its own starting speed, Alder Park improved more than any other center did, while the two centers that began with the highest speeds improved less, relative to their own starting speeds, than the other three centers did.
answer_d: Relative to its own starting speed, Alder Park improved less than any other center did, while the two centers that began with the highest speeds improved more, relative to their own starting speeds, than the other three centers did.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it correctly describes the relative improvement shown in the table. Alder Park began with the lowest average speed (40 words per minute) and rose to 62, an increase of 55 percent of its starting speed, the largest proportional increase of the five centers (Birch Lane rose 50 percent and Cedar Hill 45 percent). Dunmore Road (25 percent) and Elm Street (27.5 percent), the two centers that began with the highest speeds, improved proportionally less than the other three centers. This pattern supports the coordinator's conclusion that the program's effect was proportionally largest where participants began lowest.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The statement is accurate, since Elm Street ended at 153 words per minute and gained 33 compared with Alder Park's 22, but it compares final speeds and absolute gains, which do not show whether the effect was proportionally largest at the center that began lowest. If anything, Alder Park's small absolute gain reflects its low starting point.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. Cedar Hill did gain the most words per minute (36), and it began below Dunmore Road and Elm Street, but this is an absolute gain at a center that did not begin with the lowest speed. Alder Park, the center that began lowest, is not addressed, so the statement does not support the conclusion.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It reverses the direction of the relationship. Alder Park's proportional increase (55 percent) was the largest, not the smallest, and the two centers that began with the highest speeds had the smallest proportional increases (25 and 27.5 percent), not the largest.

headers: Average speed at enrollment (words per minute)
Average speed after program (words per minute)
